title: Envy at work
hookLine: a colleague's success, and the price they paid for it

lines: ENVY THE ROTTENNESS OF THE BONES.
cards: The announcement goes out. Someone else got the role, the bonus, the project everyone wanted. The congratulations in the chat arrive fast, a row of little hands clapping.

Underneath, for some people, something slower starts to chew. The book of Proverbs, in the King James Bible, has a line for it: "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones."
It doesn't make a sound. It just sits in the bones. Today: muditā.

teach.b: First, an old voice that found envy inside work itself. Ecclesiastes says, "Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour."
Notice the word right: good work, done well, and the neighbor envies it. Envy isn't a sign that something went wrong at the office. It follows good work around.
Envy looks at a colleague's win and skips the bill. The promotion may have come with late nights, a move, a missed dinner, a risk that could have gone the other way. Or it may not have.
Often we simply don't know: envy works from half a picture. An honest question helps. Would I take the whole trade, price included?
If yes, that tells us what we want. If no, the envy loosens. Third, a practice from Buddhism with a name: muditā.
Buddhist teaching names it as one of four qualities to cultivate, along with loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity, and it means gladness at someone else's good fortune.
In the meditation manuals it isn't left to arrive on its own. It's practiced on purpose, bringing to mind a person who is doing well and wishing that their good fortune last.
Fourth, Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."
Rejoicing comes first in the line.
Envy says their win is my loss. These voices say their win is theirs, and a share of the gladness is free to anyone who wants it.

how: Buddhists cultivate muditā, gladness at others' good fortune, as one of the four brahmaviharas, often in meditation; Christians read Romans 12:15 as a call to share in others' joy and grief.

games.q: a colleague beside you gets the promotion you wanted. Paul's letter to the Romans has a line for it. what does it say to do first?
o: keep your distance for a while.
rejoice with them that do rejoice.
games.why: rejoicing comes first: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."

practice: Bring to mind a colleague or a friend whose success has stung a little, and notice where the sting sits without pushing it away. Allow that their win had a price, the parts nobody posts, even if you don't know what it was.
Then, the way muditā is practiced, wish them well, may this good thing stay with them, or if you pray, hold them in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Muditā. Gladness at someone else's good fortune, a quality Buddhist teaching asks us to practice on purpose. Today's word.
